{{Short description|Resemblance to reality}}
{{for multi|verisimilitude in stories|Verisimilitude (fiction)|other uses|Verisimilitude (disambiguation)}}
{{essay|date=January 2012}}

In [[philosophy]], '''verisimilitude''' (or '''truthlikeness''') is the [[Notion (philosophy)|notion]] that some [[proposition]]s are closer to being [[Truth|true]] than other propositions. The problem of verisimilitude is the problem of articulating what it takes for one false [[Philosophical theory|theory]] to be closer to the truth than another false theory.<ref>{{cite web|url = https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/truthlikeness/|title=Truthlikeness, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy|access-date=2019-10-11}}</ref>

This problem was central to the [[philosophy of science|philosophy]] of [[Karl Popper]], largely because Popper was among the first to  affirm that truth is the aim of [[Models of scientific inquiry|scientific inquiry]] while acknowledging that most of the greatest scientific theories in the [[history of science]] are, strictly speaking, false. If this long string of purportedly false theories is to constitute progress with respect to the goal of truth, then it must be at least possible for one false theory to be closer to the truth than others.

==Karl Popper==
{{see also|Karl Popper#Truth}}

Popper's formal definition of verisimilitude was challenged since 1974 by [[Pavel Tichý]],<ref>{{cite journal |author=Pavel Tichý |author-link=Pavel Tichý |title=On Popper's Definitions of Verisimilitude |journal=[[The British Journal for the Philosophy of Science]] |publisher=[[Oxford University Press]] |date=June 1974 |volume=25 |issue=2 |pages=155–160 |jstor=686819 |doi=10.1093/bjps/25.2.155}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |author=Pavel Tichý |title=Verisimilitude Redefined  |journal=The British Journal for the Philosophy of Science |date=March 1976 |volume=27 |issue=1 |pages=25–42 |jstor=686376 |doi=10.1093/bjps/27.1.25}}</ref> [[John Henry Harris (philosopher)|John Henry Harris]],<ref>{{cite journal |author=John H. Harris |author-link=John Henry Harris (philosopher) |title=Popper's Definitions of 'Verisimilitude' |journal=The British Journal for the Philosophy of Science |date=June 1974 |volume=25 |issue=2 |pages=160–166 |jstor=686820 |doi=10.1093/bjps/25.2.160}}</ref> and [[David Miller (philosopher)|David Miller]],<ref>{{cite journal |author=David Miller |author-link=David Miller (philosopher) |title=Popper's Qualitative Theory of Verisimilitude |journal=The British Journal for the Philosophy of Science |date=June 1974 |volume=25 |issue=2 |pages=166–177 |jstor=686821 |doi=10.1093/bjps/25.2.166}}</ref> who argued that Popper's definition has an [[unintended consequences|unintended consequence]]: that no false theory can be closer to the truth than another. Popper himself stated: "I accepted the criticism of my definition within minutes of its presentation, wondering why I had not seen the mistake before."<ref>{{cite book |author=Karl Popper |author-link=Karl Popper |editor=W. W. Bartley III |editor-link=W. W. Bartley III |title=Realism and the Aim of Science. From the Postscript to the Logic of Scientific Discovery |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=tlowU8nS2ygC |year=2013 |orig-date=1983 |publisher=[[Routledge]] |location=[[Abingdon-on-Thames]] |isbn=978-1-1358-5895-7 |page=[https://books.google.com/books?id=tlowU8nS2ygC&dq=%22I+accepted+the+criticism+of+my+definition+within+minutes+of+its+presentation,+wondering+why+I+had+not+seen+the+mistake+before%22&pg=PR36 xxxvi]}}</ref> This result gave rise to a search for an account of verisimilitude that did not deem progress towards the truth an impossibility.

==Post-Popperian theories==

Theories proposed by David Miller and by [[Theo Kuipers]] build on Popper's approach, guided by the notion that truthlikeness is a function of a truth factor and a content factor. Others (e.g. those advanced by {{ill|Gerhard Schurz|de}} in collaboration with {{ill|Paul Weingartner|de}}, by Mortensen, and by [[Ken Gemes]]) are also inspired by Popper's approach but locate what they believe to be the error of Popper's proposal in his overly generous notion of content, or consequence, proposing instead that the consequences that contribute to closeness to truth must be, in a technical sense, "relevant". A different approach (already proposed by [[Pavel Tichý|Tichý]] and {{ill|Risto Hilpinen|fi}} and developed especially by [[Ilkka Niiniluoto]] and [[Graham Oddie]]) takes the "likeness" in truthlikeness literally, holding that a proposition's likeness to the truth is a function of the overall likeness to the actual world of the possible worlds in which the proposition would be true. An attempt to use the notion of point-free metric space is proposed by Giangiacomo Gerla.<ref>{{cite book|first=Graham |last=Oddie|title= Truthlikeness|work=Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy|year=2016|publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University|url= http://plato.stanford.edu/entries/truthlikeness/}}</ref> There is currently a debate about whether or to what extent these different approaches to the concept are compatible.<ref>{{cite journal | author = Zwart S. D., Franssen M. | year = 2007 | title = An impossibility theorem for verisimilitude | url = https://repository.tudelft.nl/islandora/object/uuid%3A6aeb2104-e4ce-452c-a141-a47c6d93c9c3/datastream/OBJ/download| journal = Synthese | volume = 158 | issue = 1| pages = 75–92 | doi=10.1007/s11229-006-9051-y| s2cid = 28812992 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | author = Oddie Graham | year = 2013 | title = The content, consequence and likeness approaches to verisimilitude: compatibility, trivialization, and underdetermination | journal = Synthese | volume = 190 | issue = 9| pages = 1647–1687 | doi=10.1007/s11229-011-9930-8| s2cid = 15527839 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | author = Gerla G | year = 2007 | title = Point free geometry and verisimilitude of theories | journal = Journal of Philosophical Logic | volume = 36 | issue = 6| pages = 707–733 | doi=10.1007/s10992-007-9059-x| s2cid = 29922810 }}</ref>
